what_the_class_is: Not where a filter section sits or how wide it is, but how the byte that says how far up or down it goes reaches it. Every model in this archive has assumed one answer without asking: that the section is built at the gain the byte names. There is a second answer the era has better reasons for, and the two agree at both ends of the byte's range and nowhere between -- which is why nothing noticed. Four slots of the standalone equaliser take such a byte and one of them was read at every setting it has.

era.when: Mid nineteen-nineties, a custom fixed-point DSP with a small control processor beside it.
what_that_implies: Building a section at an arbitrary gain is the expensive answer and it is expensive twice over. The coefficients want a sine and a square root of the gain, which the control processor would rather not run on every parameter change; storing them instead costs a coefficient set per setting, and a gain that answers over twenty-five values is twenty-five sets per entry of the tables beside it.

Blending one stored section against the dry path is the cheap answer, and in coefficients it is not a blend at all. Mixing `b/a` towards unity gives `((1-m)a + m b)/a`: the denominator never moves and the numerator is three multiply-accumulates between two stored rows. One section per entry of the frequency and width tables, one multiplier per setting of the gain.

A cut is a coefficient swap. The peaking section every filter cookbook of the period prints turns a boost into a cut by exchanging its numerator and its denominator, so a part that has the boost has the cut for nothing and does not store a second section for it. The alternative -- a second stored section at full cut, blended towards -- is what a constant-width graphic equaliser does, and it is the reason those are known for cutting narrower than they boost.

The gain law and the path are separate questions. What the byte asks for is a decibel a step over a window of twenty-five values, which is measured and closed; how what it asks for reaches the section is this one. A blend solved against the section it blends towards asks for the same decibels either way.
era.would_be_wrong_if: The section at half its full gain had the width its width byte asks for, read at a resolution the run can tell apart -- which is what it would have if the section were built at the gain.

candidates.what: The section is the cookbook section computed at the gain the byte names, whether that is done on the fly or read out of a set stored per setting. What every model here has assumed.

predicts.the_width_at_half_gain: The width the width byte asks for, the same at every setting of the gain.
predicts.the_shape_at_the_ends: The same as every other candidate: at full gain all of them are one section.
predicts.the_residual_against_a_fine_gain_sweep: Flat in the gain. A model of this shape is as right at six decibels as at twelve.

candidates.what: One section stored at the top of the printed range, blended against the dry path by a multiplier the byte selects, with a cut the same blend inverted.

predicts.the_width_at_half_gain: Narrower than the width byte asks for, by about forty per cent on a peak at half of twelve decibels -- because the half-gain points the width is defined at move inwards as the peak shrinks while the stored shape does not.
predicts.the_shape_at_the_ends: As above, and at the byte's centre too: the blend is nothing there.
predicts.the_residual_against_a_fine_gain_sweep: Nothing at both ends and at the centre, and largest between them, which is a shape no monotone lean test sees.

candidates.what: The same blend, with the cut side blending towards a second section stored at full cut rather than inverting the boost.

predicts.the_width_at_half_gain: Narrower on the boost side exactly as above, and wider on the cut side -- half the boost's width at six decibels down.
predicts.the_shape_at_the_ends: The same as the others again.
predicts.the_residual_against_a_fine_gain_sweep: The same hump on the boost side and a larger one of the opposite sense on the cut side, so the two blends are told apart by a cut and not by a boost.

what_no_candidate_here_predicts: How many coefficient sets are stored. A section computed on the fly at the gain asked for and a set stored for each of the twenty-five settings give the same curve at every setting, so no reading of this unit's output separates them. That is a difference in ROM and the class says so rather than choosing.

What the byte asks for. A decibel a step over a window of twenty-five values with both ends clamped is a closed claim of its own, and every candidate here takes it from there rather than fitting it. A blend is solved against the section it blends towards, so all three stand where the byte asked and differ only in shape.
Whether the same path serves a stage that is not a filter. A balance, a level and a send all have a byte that says how far up something goes and none of them has a section for it to reach.
What happens past the window. Every candidate here inherits the clamp, which was measured fifty steps out on two types.
note: The reading that separates these is the width of the feature at a gain in the middle of the window, and it is nearly free: the archive already holds a gain byte swept at every one of the thirty-three values between the window's ends and four steps past each of them. What it costs is asking the residual a question it has not been asked, because a residual meaned over a record is smallest where the candidates differ most -- the settings in the middle of a gain window are the settings whose profile is smallest, so they carry the least of the record's own span.
